paragraphs: An agent in a Markov decision process chooses actions to improve its own rewards. Those choices can also impose costs or create benefits outside the agent’s objective. This paper studies how a designer can account for those external effects by changing parameters that influence rewards, environmental transitions, or both.

The authors express this interaction as a two-level optimization problem. At the lower level, the agent solves its decision problem under the current model. At the upper level, the designer chooses how that model should change. This structure makes the agent’s response part of the design problem: changing incentives or dynamics can change which behavior the agent prefers.

Their algorithm repeatedly solves the agent’s decision problem to predict its reaction, then updates the model parameters using that prediction. The paper provides a theoretical analysis and empirical tests on models from economics and robotics. Its contribution is a concrete framework for adapting an environment’s rules while explicitly accounting for the behavior those rules induce.
icml-2022-adaptive-model-design-for-mark.tldr: The paper develops a two-level optimization method for redesigning rewards and dynamics around an agent’s predicted response.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve decisions using an existing dataset, even when that dataset covers only part of the possible behavior. ATAC addresses this setting through relative pessimism: it evaluates a proposed policy against the policy that collected the data, looking for plausible reasons the proposal could perform worse.

The method casts learning as a two-player Stackelberg game between an actor and a value critic. The actor proposes a policy, while the adversarially trained critic searches for scenarios consistent with the data in which that policy loses to the behavior policy. This makes the comparison with existing behavior central to the learning objective.

The guarantees require the actor to attain no regret in this game. Under that condition, ATAC outperforms the behavior policy across a broad range of pessimism settings; with appropriately chosen settings, it also competes with the best policy covered by the data. The paper supports general function approximation theoretically and supplies a scalable deep-learning implementation. On the reported D4RL continuous-control tasks, ATAC consistently exceeds the compared state-of-the-art offline methods.
icml-2022-adversarially-trained-actor-cr.tldr: ATAC trains an actor against a pessimistic critic to improve offline policies relative to the behavior represented in their data.

paragraphs: Auxiliary learning uses additional tasks to help solve a target task. Choosing which tasks matter is only part of the problem: individual examples within the same auxiliary task can contribute very differently. This paper argues that overlooking those differences wastes useful information and makes learning less robust to noisy data.

The proposed joint task and data scheduling model, JTDS, learns how much importance to assign at both levels. Its scheduler maps task information, input features, and labels into a schedule. This shared mapping addresses the parameter burden that would arise from learning a large collection of scheduling decisions separately.

Training uses two linked optimization levels. The task model learns through gradients adjusted by the schedule, while the scheduler learns through an implicit gradient that accounts for the task-learning process. In the reported experiments, JTDS significantly outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods in supervised, semi-supervised, and corrupted-label settings. The findings support treating the usefulness of an auxiliary example as something to learn jointly with the usefulness of its task.
icml-2022-auxiliary-learning-with-joint-.tldr: JTDS improves auxiliary learning by jointly learning which tasks and which examples should influence the target model.

paragraphs: A sparse subnetwork extracted from a pretrained model can sometimes retain the full model’s ability to transfer to new tasks. This paper asks for a stronger result: preserving both ordinary predictive performance and adversarial robustness. It calls subnetworks meeting these requirements double-win lottery tickets.

The definition covers transfer under both standard and adversarial training. A qualifying subnetwork must independently reach the full pretrained model’s standard and robust generalization across diverse downstream tasks. The authors compare different pretraining mechanisms and find that robust pretraining tends to yield sparser qualifying subnetworks with better performance than standard pretraining.

For transfer from ImageNet to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, adversarial pretraining yields reported matching subnetworks at 91.41% and 83.22% sparsity, respectively. The study also observes that these subnetworks can transfer more efficiently when downstream data are scarce, including settings using 1% or 10% of the data. These findings suggest that robust pretraining’s benefits can become more pronounced when combined with subnetwork selection and limited transfer data.
icml-2022-data-efficient-double-win-lott.tldr: Robust pretraining can yield sparse subnetworks that preserve both standard and adversarial transfer performance while using limited downstream data efficiently.

paragraphs: Detecting anomalies in several sensor streams requires understanding both how each stream changes over time and how sensors relate to one another. This paper develops a probabilistic model that represents these dependencies together with the randomness present in multivariate time series. The aim is to learn useful representations of normal behavior.

The model combines an embedding-guided generative network with an adaptive variational graph convolutional recurrent network. The graph component captures relationships across sensors, while the recurrent component captures temporal relationships. Extending this construction into a deeper variational network creates multiple levels of hidden representation, allowing different layers to capture different levels of information and supporting robustness to noisy series.

The authors also introduce an upward-downward inference procedure for estimating the hidden variables. It uses both forecasting losses and reconstruction losses, so representation learning considers predicting observations as well as explaining observed data. The abstract reports accurate posterior approximation, improved representations, and experimental superiority over the compared state-of-the-art methods. The central contribution is the coordinated modeling of sensor relationships, temporal structure, and uncertainty.
icml-2022-deep-variational-graph-convolu.tldr: A deep probabilistic graph-recurrent model combines sensor dependencies, temporal patterns, and hierarchical hidden representations for time-series anomaly detection.

paragraphs: Optimal transport relates the cost of moving or matching probability mass to the resulting allocation. Inverse optimal transport asks the reverse question: given an observed coupling between two probability distributions, what underlying costs could explain it? Such couplings can describe outcomes in matching problems or the movement of distributions.

This paper develops a systematic mathematical treatment of the inverse problem using tools from entropy-regularized optimal transport. A central result characterizes a manifold of cross-ratio equivalent costs, describing a structured collection of costs with the relevant equivalence property. This makes the relationships among possible cost explanations an explicit object of study.

The authors also analyze how model priors affect the inverse problem and derive a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler for probabilistic inference. Their empirical work includes visual examples of cross-ratio equivalence, simulations checking the theoretical results, and experiments with real-world data. The contribution brings together mathematical structure and a sampling procedure, giving the inverse problem a more developed foundation for reasoning about costs behind observed couplings.
icml-2022-discrete-probabilistic-inverse.tldr: The paper develops theory and probabilistic sampling methods for inferring transport costs from observed couplings.

paragraphs: Domain generalization trains on available source domains without access to the target domain. This makes it difficult to preserve features that will distinguish classes in the unseen setting. The paper studies classifier ensembles as a response to model misspecification and develops a theoretical connection between ensemble diversity and target-domain risk.

Using a pruned Jensen-Shannon loss, the authors bound an ensemble’s target square-root risk through averaged source square-root risks of sampled classifiers. They obtain a tighter bound by enforcing a particular positive diversity measure, then derive a PAC-Bayes upper bound. The relevance of diversity is therefore tied to a specified mathematical measure and risk formulation.

Their diversified neural averaging method approximately optimizes this bound. It draws classifier variation from both dropout and different points along the optimization trajectory. To keep prediction inexpensive, it approximates the ensemble by averaging weights across training with dropout disabled, using a single run. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art classification performance on standard domain-generalization benchmarks, supporting the practical value of this theoretically motivated averaging approach.
icml-2022-dna-domain-generalization-with.tldr: DNA uses a diversity-sensitive generalization bound to guide efficient neural averaging for unseen target domains.

paragraphs: Machine-learning APIs differ in both price and accuracy, making the best choice depend on a user’s data and budget. The problem becomes harder when an input can have many labels, as in text or multi-object recognition. Earlier selection approaches for single-label APIs have computation costs that grow exponentially with the number of labels.

FrugalMCT addresses this problem by choosing APIs adaptively as data arrive, subject to the user’s budget. It can combine predictions from multiple APIs for a single input. An accuracy estimator guides the choice of combination, allowing the framework to make different service choices for different data points.

The authors evaluate services from several providers on multi-label image classification, scene text recognition, and named entity recognition. Across these tasks, they report that FrugalMCT can reduce cost by more than 90% while matching the best single API’s accuracy, or improve accuracy by up to 8% at that API’s cost. These are alternative observed tradeoffs, showing how adaptive selection and combination can improve the usefulness of existing services.
icml-2022-efficient-online-ml-api-select.tldr: FrugalMCT adaptively selects and combines classification APIs to improve accuracy-cost tradeoffs within a user’s budget.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether classic graph algorithms can run faster when supplied with predictions learned from past or similar problems. The predictions serve as additional advice to an algorithm. The goal is to improve on traditional worst-case runtime guarantees by using information that the ordinary problem input does not provide.

The authors develop a faster minimum-weight bipartite matching algorithm using learned dual information. They extend the same approach to finding shortest paths from one source when edges may have negative lengths. For that problem, sufficiently accurate predictions enable an almost-linear runtime. Prediction quality is therefore an explicit condition of this speed claim.

The paper also presents a reduction-based framework that transfers these ideas to degree-constrained subgraphs and minimum-cost 0-1 flow through matching and shortest-path problems. Finally, general learnability theorems establish that the required predictions can be learned efficiently in the PAC framework. Together, these results address both sides of the proposal: how algorithms benefit from advice and how the needed advice can be learned.
icml-2022-faster-fundamental-graph-algor.tldr: Learned predictions accelerate several fundamental graph algorithms, including almost-linear shortest paths when predictions are sufficiently accurate.

paragraphs: Transformers use attention masks to structure interactions among positions, but incorporating different masking rules efficiently can require different methods. This paper proposes a common approach for scalable masked attention. Its organizing idea is to treat masking as a graph-based modulation of attention that would otherwise be unmasked.

Within this formulation, existing results for linear causal attention and log-linear attention with relative positional encoding become special cases. The framework also yields efficient masking methods for relative positional encoding in multiple dimensions and for graph kernels. This gives the approach value both as a unification of earlier techniques and as a route to additional masking mechanisms.

The authors draw on spectral analysis, dynamic programming, random walks, and new algorithms for Markov processes on graphs. These mathematical tools connect the structure of a mask with ways to compute attention efficiently. The paper includes an empirical evaluation alongside the theoretical development. Its stated contribution is a broad framework for scalable masking, with several concrete mechanisms obtained from the same graph-based perspective.
icml-2022-from-block-toeplitz-matrices-t.tldr: A graph-based formulation unifies scalable Transformer masking methods and enables efficient multidimensional positional and graph-kernel masks.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in which a human compares pairs of trajectories instead of supplying a numerical reward at every step. The agent seeks the policy the human most prefers. The theoretical challenge is to support general function approximation, extending analysis beyond settings represented by tables of states and actions.

The proposed algorithm learns an environment model through value-targeted regression and selects exploratory policies through optimistic planning. The authors prove a regret bound that grows with the square root of the number of episodes, apart from logarithmic factors, multiplied by a polynomial in model complexity and planning horizon. The complexity term depends on properties of both transition and preference models.

A lower bound indicates that the algorithm is near-optimal when specialized to the linear setting. The paper also introduces comparisons involving n alternatives and provides a sample-efficient algorithm for that setting. Its contribution is a theoretical account of learning from trajectory preferences with rich function classes, together with an extension beyond pairwise feedback. The near-optimality claim specifically concerns the linear specialization.
icml-2022-human-in-the-loop-provably-eff.tldr: The paper gives regret guarantees for preference-based reinforcement learning with general function approximation and extends learning to n-wise comparisons.

paragraphs: Single-point zeroth-order optimization makes progress using just one function-value query at each time step. This is useful for online black-box optimization and control in changing environments, where repeated evaluations may be impractical. Its basic form, however, has high estimation variance and converges slowly, restricting its practical usefulness.

The authors introduce HLF-SZO by borrowing high-pass and low-pass filters from extremum seeking control, a continuous-time counterpart of this optimization approach. They show that the high-pass component coincides with residual feedback, while the low-pass component can be understood as momentum. These connections explain the proposed method in terms of recognizable optimization mechanisms.

Combining the filters yields substantially lower variance and faster convergence than vanilla single-point optimization. Extensive numerical experiments verify those improvements and show empirical advantages over the residual-feedback method as well. The contribution is a way to improve the quality and usefulness of updates while retaining the single-query setting. The comparison with residual feedback is specifically an experimental finding about adding the combined filtering approach.
icml-2022-improve-single-point-zeroth-or.tldr: HLF-SZO combines residual-feedback and momentum-like filters to reduce variance and accelerate optimization using one function query per step.

paragraphs: Certifying a neural network’s robustness can be computationally difficult because large networks contain many nonlinear operations. This paper studies how to reduce that burden while preserving predictive performance. Its approach, linearity grafting, selectively replaces insignificant ReLU activations with linear functions.

After choosing which neurons to linearize, the method learns the slopes and intercepts of their replacement functions. This gives the network room to recover performance while retaining the certification benefits of greater linearity. Ordinary neuron pruning fits within this view as the special case where both slope and intercept are fixed to zero, leaving less flexibility.

Experiments across datasets and network architectures report tighter certified bounds and competitive certifiable robustness without certified robust training, including improvements exceeding 30% on CIFAR-10 models. The method also scales complete verification to large adversarially trained models with 17 million parameters. These findings support selective linearization as a way to manage the tension between expressive nonlinear models and tractable robustness certification, with learned replacements preserving more flexibility than simply removing neurons.
icml-2022-linearity-grafting-relaxed-neu.tldr: Linearity grafting replaces selected ReLUs with learned linear functions to make robustness certification more scalable while preserving model performance.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often capture only limited-range relationships because repeated aggregation can make node representations overly similar. Graph Implicit Nonlinear Diffusion, or GIND, addresses this over-smoothing problem with an implicit graph convolution. It has access to arbitrarily many neighborhood hops while adapting feature aggregation through nonlinear diffusion.

The authors show that the resulting representation is the minimizer of an explicit convex optimization objective. This provides a mathematical description of the model’s equilibrium. It also creates a design mechanism: modifying the objective produces structural variants that can incorporate prior properties into the equilibrium or introduce skip connections to improve training stability.

Experiments show that GIND captures long-range dependencies and performs well on graphs whose connected nodes tend to be similar as well as graphs whose connected nodes tend to differ. The optimization-derived variants can further improve performance, stability, and efficiency. The reported gains cover both node-level and graph-level tasks, linking the equilibrium formulation to practical improvements across different graph prediction settings.
icml-2022-optimization-induced-graph-imp.tldr: GIND uses an optimization-defined nonlinear diffusion equilibrium to capture distant graph relationships while addressing over-smoothing.

paragraphs: This paper develops classical dynamic data structures for recommendation and least-squares regression with query capabilities comparable to quantum counterparts. It contributes to de-quantization: understanding how classical methods can reproduce capabilities associated with quantum algorithms. The authors obtain sharper bounds for these problems.

The key observation is that earlier quantum-inspired methods implicitly perform leverage-score or ridge-leverage-score sampling. These are established techniques from randomized numerical linear algebra. Recognizing that connection allows the authors to use an existing body of mathematical results and algorithmic tools to improve the data structures.

The resulting algorithms are simpler, faster, or both compared with previous approaches, and experiments show that the proposed structures work well on real-world datasets. The broader methodological contribution is the identification of a familiar sampling principle beneath seemingly specialized quantum-inspired procedures. That connection explains where improvements can come from and makes numerical linear algebra directly useful in developing stronger classical solutions for the two application areas studied.
icml-2022-quantum-inspired-algorithms-fr.tldr: Recognizing standard sampling techniques inside quantum-inspired algorithms yields simpler or faster classical methods for recommendation and regression.

paragraphs: Many causal and policy quantities are linear functionals of a regression function: they summarize that function into a particular effect of interest. Regularization and model selection can bias a direct estimate of such a quantity. This paper automates the learning of a Riesz representation, which supplies information needed for a debiasing correction.

The method requires only black-box access to evaluate the linear functional, without knowing its analytic formula. RieszNet jointly learns the regression function and its Riesz representer through a combined loss, sharing neural-network representation layers. ForestRiesz instead uses a random forest to learn a locally linear representation of the Riesz function.

This design makes automatic correction available through two different learning architectures within the paper’s linear-functional setting. Experiments find good performance against a state-of-the-art neural method for average treatment effects. The authors also evaluate average marginal effects for continuous treatments using semi-synthetic data on gasoline prices and demand. These applications demonstrate the procedure on distinct effect-estimation problems while retaining the same underlying debiasing idea.
icml-2022-riesznet-and-forestriesz-autom.tldr: RieszNet and ForestRiesz learn debiasing corrections for causal and policy quantities using only black-box evaluations of the target linear functional.

paragraphs: Few-shot meta-learning must learn from very small task datasets, making it vulnerable to overfitting even when labels are correct. The paper treats this as sampling noise and separately addresses the additional disruption caused by incorrect labels. Eigen-Reptile aims to make meta-learning updates more robust to both sources of noise.

The method updates shared meta-parameters using the main direction in the history of task-specific parameters. Its computation uses a matrix whose size depends on the number of task-specific gradient steps rather than the number of model parameters. This is an important part of making the direction calculation fast for parameter-rich models.

When many labels are noisy, the authors add Introspective Self-paced Learning to obtain a more accurate main direction. They provide theoretical and experimental support for Eigen-Reptile and this additional method. Across the evaluated tasks, the approach either outperforms other gradient-based methods or achieves highly competitive performance, with and without label noise. The results support using the direction of task adaptation as a basis for more robust meta-updates.
icml-2022-robust-meta-learning-with-samp.tldr: Eigen-Reptile uses the main direction of task-specific parameter histories to improve few-shot meta-learning under sampling and label noise.

paragraphs: Decentralized actor-critic learning coordinates multiple agents toward a joint control policy. Existing methods can require sharing sensitive local information or incur substantial communication costs. This paper develops actor-critic and natural actor-critic algorithms that share only noisy rewards while using local mini-batch policy-gradient updates.

For natural actor-critic, the authors additionally develop decentralized stochastic gradient descent for Markovian data with an adaptive mini-batch size. This component computes the natural policy gradient efficiently. Together, the local updates and specialized gradient computation address the amount of data and communication needed during learning.

The theoretical results assume Markovian sampling and linear function approximation. Under those conditions, the sample-complexity bounds are O(ε^-2 log(1/ε)) for actor-critic and O(ε^-3 log(1/ε)) for natural actor-critic, with improved communication complexity of O(ε^-1 log(1/ε)). Numerical experiments also show lower sample and communication requirements than existing decentralized actor-critic methods. The contribution combines finite-time guarantees with a communication design that avoids sharing agents’ local information directly.
icml-2022-sample-and-communication-effic.tldr: Decentralized actor-critic methods use noisy reward sharing and mini-batch updates to improve sample and communication efficiency under stated approximation assumptions.

paragraphs: Private inference runs predictions directly on cryptographically protected data, but its runtime can be extremely high. The relevant computational bottleneck differs from ordinary inference: nonlinear functions such as ReLU dominate latency. This paper therefore targets the number and placement of nonlinear activations as a route to faster private prediction.

The authors propose a gradient-based method that selectively turns ReLUs into linear operations while maintaining prediction accuracy. This adjusts the network around the costs of private execution. The optimization seeks useful accuracy-latency tradeoffs by deciding which nonlinearities the model can give up.

On standard private-inference benchmarks, the method reports up to 4.25% higher accuracy at a fixed count of 50,000 ReLUs, or 2.2 times lower latency at a fixed accuracy of 70%, compared with the current state of the art. These are separate comparison settings. A complementary no-free-lunch theorem examines how and when linearization can preserve accuracy, connecting the empirical improvements to theoretical constraints on removing network nonlinearity.
icml-2022-selective-network-linearizatio.tldr: Selective ReLU linearization improves the accuracy-latency tradeoff of neural inference on cryptographically protected data.

paragraphs: This paper presents self-supervised speech learning in which a model predicts discrete labels for masked speech signals. The labels come from a simple random-projection quantizer. This provides a prediction target for learning from speech without requiring the quantizer itself to learn a representation.

The quantizer first projects speech inputs through a randomly initialized matrix, then assigns labels through nearest-neighbor lookup in a randomly initialized codebook. Both components remain fixed throughout self-supervised learning. Separating this fixed label generator from the speech-recognition model makes the approach flexible and compatible with a universal speech-recognition architecture.

On LibriSpeech, the method achieves word-error rates similar to earlier self-supervised work with non-streaming models and lower rates than earlier work with streaming models. On multilingual tasks, it also delivers significant improvements over wav2vec 2.0 and w2v-BERT. The results show that a fixed random quantizer can supply effective training targets in these settings, with the reported advantages depending on the recognition setting and comparison.
icml-2022-self-supervised-learning-with-.tldr: A fixed random-projection quantizer supplies effective masked-prediction targets for self-supervised speech recognition.

paragraphs: Linear contextual bandits support personalized decisions while learning from user information. Privacy guarantees depend on who must be trusted: central privacy relies on the server, while local privacy protects information on the user’s side but can reduce learning utility. This paper investigates an intermediate arrangement using a trusted shuffler.

The shuffler randomly permutes batches of user data before forwarding them to the server. The authors propose a general bandit framework for this trust model and instantiate it with two protocols. One amplifies the privacy of local mechanisms through shuffling; the other uses a protocol for summing bounded vectors and matrices.

Both versions improve regret guarantees over the local model. When every user is unique, regret can potentially scale as T^(3/5), ignoring logarithmic factors, compared with the cited local-model rate of T^(3/4). Synthetic simulations support the regret behavior. For repeated users, the paper establishes a T^(2/3) rate up to logarithmic factors, matching the central model’s achievable rate in that setting. The trusted shuffler remains an explicit part of the arrangement.
icml-2022-shuffle-private-linear-context.tldr: A trusted shuffler enables private contextual-bandit learning with stronger trust requirements than central privacy and improved regret over local privacy.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks offer an event-driven computing approach suited to energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware. As their performance improves through deeper and more flexible structures, parameter counts and computational burdens also grow. This paper develops a pruning method inspired by the changing states of dendritic spines.

The method assigns different states to network weights and uses a nonlinear mapping from spine size to weight value. State-transition thresholds grow during learning, and different growth functions control how quickly pruning proceeds. These elements form a dynamic pruning algorithm that couples weight optimization with the progression toward a sparse network.

For SEW ResNet18 on ImageNet, the authors report 88.8% sparsity with a 3% performance loss, described as state-of-the-art low loss compared with existing pruning methods for directly trained spiking networks. They also find that regulating pruning speed during learning is crucial to avoiding severe degradation late in training. The result emphasizes that the timing of pruning, alongside the weight-state model, matters for retaining performance.
icml-2022-state-transition-of-dendritic-.tldr: A dendritic-spine-inspired weight model enables dynamic pruning of spiking networks, with pruning speed crucial to preserving late-training performance.

paragraphs: Local differential privacy protects user data by randomizing information before it is used. For data with many attributes, task-agnostic methods can substantially harm prediction because they add noise without considering which features matter to the eventual task. This paper makes that task relevance part of the privacy mechanism’s design.

The proposed encoder-decoder framework learns a hidden representation of user data that is relevant to the task and anonymizes that representation. This ties the information being protected to the information needed for prediction. The authors obtain an analytical near-optimal solution for a linear setting with mean-squared-error task loss.

For general nonlinear settings, they provide an approximate solution learned with gradients. Experiments show significant gains in final task accuracy over standard local-differential-privacy benchmarks at the same level of privacy guarantee. The findings support adapting the representation to the task as a way to improve utility within a fixed privacy requirement. The near-optimal analytical claim applies specifically to the linear, mean-squared-error setting.
icml-2022-task-aware-privacy-preservatio.tldr: Learning and anonymizing task-relevant representations improves prediction accuracy at the same local differential privacy guarantee.

paragraphs: Point-cloud recognition models can be misled by semantic transformations such as rotations or tapering, even when the changes are designed to be subtle. This paper introduces TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing framework that provides robustness certificates against such attacks. The goal is to make guarantees both tight and scalable.

TPC first divides transformations into composable and indirectly composable categories, using rotation and tapering as examples. It develops a general certification strategy for each category, then derives specialized protocols for particular transformations. This organization lets the mathematical treatment reflect the structure of the transformation being certified.

Experiments across several common three-dimensional transformations show substantial improvements over the compared state-of-the-art method. For twisting around the z-axis within plus or minus 20 degrees, the reported certified accuracy rises from 20.3% to 83.8%. This result concerns accuracy accompanied by a robustness guarantee for the specified transformation range. The contribution combines a general categorization with transformation-specific analysis to strengthen certification for point-cloud models.
icml-2022-tpc-transformation-specific-sm.tldr: TPC tailors smoothing-based certification to individual 3D transformations, substantially improving reported point-cloud robustness guarantees.

paragraphs: Routed language models use only a subset of their parameters for each input. This separates total model capacity from the computation used to process an input. The paper studies how performance scales along these two independent axes, extending scaling laws that describe standard language models primarily through parameter count.

The authors derive and justify laws that describe a broad range of routing architectures trained with three different techniques. These laws account jointly for model size and computational requirements. Their analysis draws on evaluations spanning five orders of magnitude in size, including models with hundreds of experts and hundreds of billions of parameters.

The paper applies the laws in two ways. It defines an effective parameter count under which the studied models scale at the same rate, giving a shared basis for comparison. It also uses the fitted scaling coefficients to compare the three routing techniques quantitatively. The contribution is a unified account of how conditional parameter use changes the relationship among capacity, computation, and language-model performance.
icml-2022-unified-scaling-laws-for-route.tldr: Two-variable scaling laws describe routed language-model performance through both total parameters and computation, enabling comparisons across routing techniques.
